column10: RuleApiKey has all fields optional (id?, name?, key?) even though the API always returns them. This forces unnecessary optional chaining in all consumer code and defeats TypeScript's static guarantees. Fields like `id`, `name`, and `key` should be required, matching the pattern of RuleAccount (which has `id: number`). The `key` field is particularly important since it's the primary purpose of this type — consumers calling `result.data?.key` should not have to handle `undefined`.

RuleBrandStyleManualRequest is being exported as a @deprecated type alias in the same PR that introduces it — it has never existed as a non-deprecated public API. Per the project's own rule ("Every public export is a contract"), this creates permanent API surface that must be maintained forever, but it was never useful to consumers. The backward-compat fiction doesn't hold because there was no prior published release using this type. It should not be exported.

RuleBrandStyleManualRequest is re-exported from the public entry point despite being @deprecated from the moment it was introduced in this PR. Exporting a deprecated type with no prior usage creates unnecessary permanent API surface. See also src/types/api.ts:955-957.

The `fonts` array in RuleBrandStyleCreateRequest (and RuleBrandStyleUpdateRequest at line 940) requires `origin: RuleBrandStyleFontOrigin` (non-optional), but the response type RuleBrandStyleFont (line 842) has `origin?: RuleBrandStyleFontOrigin | null`. This asymmetry means that fonts returned by the API (which may have `origin: null` for system fonts) cannot be used directly in a subsequent update call — TypeScript will error because `origin` is required in the request but the value in hand is `undefined | null`. Either the request type should allow `origin` to be optional, or the response type should make it required.

listBrandStyles() accepts no pagination parameters, unlike every other list method in the SDK (listAutomails, listMessages, listTemplates, etc., all accept page/per_page via RulePaginationParams). If an account has many brand styles, there is no way to paginate through them. This inconsistency will become a breaking change to add later.

listApiKeys() accepts no pagination parameters, unlike other list methods in the SDK. If the Rule.io API supports pagination on this endpoint, callers have no way to control it. This inconsistency is also a breaking API change to fix after the fact.

The `fonts` array in RuleBrandStyleUpdateRequest requires `origin: RuleBrandStyleFontOrigin` (non-optional), but the response type RuleBrandStyleFont has `origin?: RuleBrandStyleFontOrigin | null`. Same roundtrip asymmetry as in CreateRequest (line 916): a PATCH to partially update fonts using data fetched from the API would require manually adding `origin` even for fonts where the API returned it as null.

updateBrandStyle() does not handle 404 — it throws a RuleApiError if the brand style ID does not exist. This is inconsistent with getBrandStyle() which returns null on 404. A caller that fetched a brand style (possibly returning null) and then tries to update it using the same ID would get an exception rather than a consistent null-means-not-found semantic. Consider either returning null on 404 (consistent with the getter) or documenting that update throws where get would return null.

The `updateApiKey` method uses `PUT`, but a `PUT` request typically implies a full replacement of the resource. The `RuleApiKeyUpdateRequest` only allows updating the `name` field, and the API probably uses `PATCH` for partial updates, consistent with `updateBrandStyle`. Using `PUT` here could unintentionally clear other fields on the API key resource if the backend strictly follows REST conventions for `PUT`.

In `getBrandStyle`, the return type is `Promise<RuleBrandStyleResponse | null>`, which is a wrapper object. However, the `catch` block returns `null` directly, not a wrapper object. Callers expecting a `RuleBrandStyleResponse` object with a `data` property will get a `TypeError` when trying to access properties on `null`. The method should return `null` when an item is not found, but this type inconsistency is problematic. The JSDoc example also incorrectly accesses `.data` on a potentially null object without a check (`style.data?.colours`). A more consistent return type would be `Promise<RuleBrandStyle | null>` to align with the 404-handling behavior.

The `getBrandStyle` example code shows `console.log(style.data?.colours)`. Since the method returns `Promise<RuleBrandStyleResponse | null>`, `style` itself can be `null` if the brand style is not found (404). The example code will throw a `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'data')` in that case. It should be `if (style) { console.log(style.data?.colours); }`.

In the method `deleteBrandStyle`, it is mentioned that it throws a 403 error when deleting the last brand style, but there is no specific check for this in the implementation. This can lead to inconsistent error handling behavior.
The `updateBrandStyle` method does not perform input validation to ensure the `request` body adheres to the expected schema, potentially leading to runtime errors or unexpected API responses.
The test case `should throw on 403 when deleting last brand style` does not verify the exact error message or status code returned by the `RuleApiError`, reducing the reliability of the test.

The test case `should throw RuleApiError on 424 (failed to fetch domain)` does not validate the `error` instance for its type and message thoroughly, which could be useful for debugging and detecting regressions.
The `RuleBrandStyleUpdateRequest` definition does not enforce validation for the `name` field's length or content (e.g., max characters, disallowed characters), which could lead to API-side errors.

In the `createApiKey` operation, there is no validation for the `name` field to ensure it adheres to the API's maximum length constraint (255 characters). This could lead to server-side validation errors.
The `RuleApiKeyCreateRequest` type does not strongly validate that the `name` property is a non-empty string, potentially leading to unclear errors if `name` is omitted or invalid.
In the test `should create an API key`, the validation of the generated API key value (field `key`) is missing, which reduces its completeness and the ability to detect unexpected behavior.

This uses `requestV3`, which logs the full parsed response when `debug` is enabled. `RuleApiKey` includes the secret `key` value and the new tests model list responses containing keys, so `listApiKeys()` can leak API keys into application logs; handle this endpoint like `getAccount()` does by omitting or redacting sensitive response bodies before logging.

`createApiKey()` returns the newly generated secret key, but routing it through `requestV3` means the full response is logged whenever client debug mode is enabled. This can expose the new API key in logs; use a non-logging/redacted path for this response.

The example encourages printing the generated API key to stdout. Because this value is a secret credential, examples should avoid logging it directly to reduce the chance of leaking keys into terminal history or centralized logs.

The create and update brand-style request payload shapes duplicate the same nested `colours`, `links`, `fonts`, and `images` definitions. This makes future OpenAPI changes easy to apply to one request but miss the other; consider extracting shared input item types and composing the create/update request types so they stay in sync.

The new manual brand-style request supports custom font payloads, but the added tests never send a `fonts` entry (searched `tests/client.test.ts` and found no font coverage). Since custom font serialization is part of the new public API surface, add a test that verifies the expected font payload is sent unchanged.

The new manual brand-style request supports base64 image payloads, but the added tests never send an `images` entry (searched `tests/client.test.ts` and found no image coverage). Add coverage for image serialization so regressions in this required OpenAPI shape are caught.
